text: Paper · Preprint · arXiv 2608.14036 Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work - Until They Don't Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, Hanwen Xing, Xander Wu, Yipeng Gao, Rui Cao, Mengdi Wang, Shilong Liu, Yijiang Li Princeton, UC San Diego, Stanford, USC, Johns Hopkins (corresponding authors Mengdi Wang, Shilong Liu, Yijiang Li; Jiang worked on it as a Princeton intern) · August 2026 (arXiv v1, 14 August 2026; the only version so far) In one line: First mechanistic account of SKILL.md: identical trajectories distilled into skills beat raw workflow memory by +6.06 points because skills act as procedural anchors (not knowledge injection), but they add a new 10% misapplication failure mode, and retrieval precision decouples from downstream task success. +6.06 points Skill over Workflow Memory built from the same trajectories 95% bootstrap CI [+0.76, +11.36] over 528 paired triples; Skill over Raw is +2.84 with a CI that includes zero · Table 10 65.7% vs 4.5% of skill runs act as a procedural anchor, against supplying missing knowledge labels from one LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6); the skill arm's new failure, misapplied or ignored guidance, is 10.0% against 0.8% raw · §5.1 29.6% → 3.3% actual-use precision as the skill pool grows from 5 to 100 while downstream success moves from 36.4% to 39.3%; averages over the two agents and three distractor regimes on SkillsBench · Table 4 read it (arXiv HTML) · PDF · no code released; the replayed SkillsBench task · replay the paired run How far to trust it: Believe the direction: on most setups a distilled skill beats the same experience pasted in as workflow traces, and skills bring a misapplication failure of their own.
